gates.label: held-out recall
gates.why: A private name reaching a model is the failure this library exists to prevent, so this one is 100% and the others are allowed slack.

gates.label: held-out recall (carrier)
gates.why: The same spans inside a real essay rather than an isolated frame. Isolated frames went green while a carrier essay leaked; eight passes hid one leak.

gates.label: KEEP precision
gates.why: Recall alone rewards a redactor that masks everything. This is what stops that being a passing score.

gates.label: round-trip
gates.why: Masked text must map back one-to-one. Below 100% a student cannot be shown their own words, which is the property numbered placeholders exist for.

gates.label: unaccounted violations
gates.why: Known violations are listed with reasons. The gate is that no UNLISTED one appears, and a second test fails when a listed one stops occurring, so a stale exemption cannot shelter the next defect of the same shape.

gates.label: over-fire on prose
gates.why: Over-redaction is the cost side of recall. A FLOOR, not a rate: the measured corpus is pre-scrubbed, so real prose offers more to over-fire on. The only gate whose bar is a property of the PROSE rather than the detector, so it is set per corpus: ASAP-AES set 8 is a personal narrative whose names were already @PERSON tokens, while PERSUADE's prompts are source-based and its essays name real entities constantly (Venus, Vauban, Paris, Earth). One bar cannot hold both, and a single bar loose enough for PERSUADE would retire the gate on ASAP-AES. `bar` is the fallback for a corpus with no entry, and it is deliberately the tighter of the two so a new corpus fails loudly rather than passing quietly.

gates.label: bare-surname exposure
gates.why: How many ordinary US surnames a bare mention would keep by mistake. Watches every new single-token tier.

gates.label: latency vs last release
gates.why: How much slower this port redacts the corpus than the last release does, per implementation, with both measured on the same machine minutes apart. Two designs preceded this one and each decided a release wrongly. An absolute 10 ms bar passed on a laptop and failed on the runner enforcing it, so 0.2.3 published to PyPI and npm while RubyGems refused the same commit. A stored per-release baseline then red-lit main on unchanged code at +8.33%, because the profile it pinned — ubuntu-latest — is not a machine: 36 processes over six runners spread 67% in Ruby, 26% in Python and 21% in TypeScript on identical code, and the label served five CPU models. Timing the previous release HERE cancels every one of those terms, leaving within-process noise of 0.7-3.3%. The figure is the median of every essay x every repeat pooled — 100 samples, asset load and a full warmup pass excluded — NOT a percentile: at n=20 essays a p95 IS the maximum, and a maximum moves on a scheduling pause rather than on code. Without a paired record the gate reports NOT MEASURED and says why, because one side of a comparison is not a gate.

gates.label: asset entries
gates.why: A gazetteer that reads back empty redacts every public figure in every essay — privacy-safe, product-hostile, and invisible to every other gate.

requirements.census: US surname frequencies. `conformance/census/` ships the two columns this scores against — all 162,253 rows of the 2010 release, so the rate is identical to the upstream's to the last bearer — because census.gov stopped serving the file and this gate reported NOT MEASURED everywhere but on one machine. VICARY_EVAL_CENSUS_CSV overrides with an operator's own copy. Repository only: like the rest of conformance/, it ships in no package, and the redaction path never reads it.
requirements.corpus: An essay corpus. Which one is declared in conformance/corpora/ and selected per the registry there: VICARY_EVAL_CORPUS names one outright, else a configured VICARY_EVAL_CORPUS_TSV / _DIR keeps the operator on ASAP-AES, else the registry default. ASAP-AES is operator-supplied and not shipped by any package here; persuade-20 ships its essays, so these gates are measurable without operator setup once it becomes the default.
requirements.latency_baseline: A PAIRED measurement, taken on the machine running the gate: tools/latency_pair.py checks the previous release out of this repository's own history and times it and this checkout alternately, then leaves both numbers in a record VICARY_LATENCY_PAIR points at. Nothing is stored between releases, because a stored number assumes the machine is a constant and it is not: identical code spread 67% across six ubuntu-latest runners in Ruby, 26% in Python and 21% in TypeScript, from a runner label that served five different CPU models. Measuring both sides here cancels all of that. Without the record the number is still measured and printed — only the verdict is withheld, because one side of a comparison is not a gate.
